opus-5.5.text:
Move 78 is one of my favorite moments of the whole match, partly because of what came before it. In game two, AlphaGo played move 37, the shoulder hit on the fifth line. Our system estimated a human would play it about one in ten thousand times. Professionals initially thought it was a mistake, and a hundred or so moves later it turned out to be pivotal. It showed that AI could do something genuinely creative, something outside the patterns of thousands of years of human play.

Then in game four, Lee Sedol, under enormous pressure and down three games to none, found move 78, the wedge in the center. People called it a "divine move." Interestingly, AlphaGo had also estimated it at around one in ten thousand, so it hadn't really considered it, and it got confused for several moves afterward. That was the game he won.

What I find beautiful is the symmetry. AlphaGo pushed into new territory, and that seemed to free Lee Sedol to look at the board differently and find something brilliant himself. He said afterward that the match made him rethink what creativity in Go meant, and I think that's the deeper lesson. These systems don't have to diminish us. They can expand the space of ideas we explore. We've seen the same thing since: top Go players now study AI games, try openings once considered unorthodox, and the overall level of human play has risen.

For me that's the template for AI in science and beyond. It's not AI replacing human ingenuity. It's a tool that shows us parts of the search space we didn't know were there, and then human intuition and creativity build on that. It's a dialogue rather than a competition.

From the scientific side, move 78 was also very valuable to us. It exposed a weakness, a kind of blind spot in how the system handled very unlikely moves. That helped us improve later versions like AlphaGo Zero. So even the moment where the human won made the AI better. That back-and-forth is exactly what I hope we'll see much more of.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AlphaGo pushed into new territory, which seemed to free Lee Sedol to see the board differently and find move 78.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes human intuition and creativity building on AI, but does not identify asking the right questions as a human contribution.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, move 78 was one of those moments that I think will stay with me for the rest of my life. We were in Seoul, it was game four, and by that point AlphaGo was up three-nil, so the match was already decided. But Lee Sedol came out and played this wedge move in the middle of the board, and our own evaluation afterwards showed that AlphaGo had assessed the probability of a human playing that move at something like one in ten thousand. It was a move that, to the best of our knowledge, almost no one would have considered. And it completely confused the system. AlphaGo's value estimates went haywire for the next ten or fifteen moves, and Lee went on to win the game.

What I find so beautiful about it is the symmetry with move 37 in game two. There, AlphaGo played a shoulder hit on the fifth line that the commentators initially thought was a mistake, and that also had roughly a one in ten thousand probability of being played by a human. And it turned out to be one of the pivotal moves of the match. So you had the machine producing a kind of creativity that surprised the human experts, and then two games later you had the human, having been pushed to the absolute limit by that, reaching for something equally unexpected. I don't think Lee Sedol plays move 78 if he hasn't just spent three games being challenged by a system that was showing him the game could be thought about differently.

And that's really the pattern I hope we see more generally. The way I think about these systems is not as replacements for human ingenuity but as tools that expand the space of what we consider possible. Lee himself said afterwards that playing AlphaGo made him rethink the game, and if you look at professional Go since then, the whole style of play has shifted. People are playing moves that were considered bad form for centuries. The AI didn't make humans worse at Go. It made them more creative, and in turn the best humans found ways to find the gaps in what the AI could do. I think that's a kind of template for what we want in science as well, where the system surfaces something unexpected and the human intuition about why it matters pushes the whole field forward.

r001.rationale: The response says Lee was challenged by AlphaGo and that he likely would not have played move 78 without that experience.

r002.rationale: It credits humans with intuition and finding gaps in AI, but does not identify asking the right questions as a human contribution.

astra-6.text:
I think move 78 was a beautiful example of that. Lee Sedol had been pushed into an extraordinarily difficult position, and he found this move that was so unexpected that AlphaGo misjudged what would follow. It was a reminder of the depth of human creativity, even against a system that was playing at such a high level.

And there’s a lovely symmetry with AlphaGo’s move 37 in the second game. There, the machine played something that initially looked strange to the human experts, but turned out to be inspired. Then, in game four, Lee Sedol produced this extraordinary response of his own.

That’s the aspect I find most exciting: each can reveal possibilities the other hasn’t considered. You see something surprising, you question your assumptions, and your understanding expands. Ideally, that’s what AI should do for us—help us discover more, and become more creative ourselves.

r001.rationale: By pairing AlphaGo’s surprising move 37 with Lee Sedol’s move 78 and saying each can reveal possibilities the other has not considered, the response suggests the machine’s play may have inspired Lee.

r002.rationale: The response says surprises can lead people to question assumptions, but it does not identify asking the right questions as a human contribution to solving problems with AI tools.

sol-6.1.text:
Move 78 was a beautiful example of human creativity under pressure. Lee Sedol was three games down, playing against a system that had shown him a very unfamiliar way of playing Go, and he still found this extraordinary move. It exposed a weakness in AlphaGo’s understanding, and he went on to win that game.

What I love is the connection with AlphaGo’s move 37 in the second game. That was a move many people initially thought was a mistake, but they came to appreciate its beauty. So you had the machine offering something surprising to the human players, and then Lee Sedol responding with something that surprised the machine—and us.

For me, that’s a glimpse of what we should be aiming for: AI expanding the possibilities we can see, and human ingenuity continuing to challenge those systems. The interaction can help us discover things that neither would have found in quite the same way alone.

r001.rationale: The response links AlphaGo’s surprising play with Lee’s response, describing the machine as offering something surprising and Lee as responding with a move that surprised the machine.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify asking the right questions as a human contribution to solving problems with AI tools.
